title: Inquiry-Based Mathematics Education: a call for reform in tertiary education seems unjustified
extended_summary:
This paper critically examines claims made by proponents of inquiry-based mathematics education (IBME) in tertiary education. The authors ask whether minimally guided, inquiry-oriented approaches are actually superior to explicit instruction for novice learners, and whether such approaches help with conceptual understanding and equity. Rather than reporting a new classroom intervention, the article synthesizes and comments on prior research from cognitive science, educational psychology, and mathematics education.

The paper focuses on undergraduate mathematics contexts, where inquiry-based instruction asks students to discover or reinvent mathematics through tasks such as defining concepts, conjecturing, proving, and solving problems with reduced lecturer guidance. The setting discussed is higher education, especially tertiary mathematics instruction in Anglosphere countries, with examples drawn from large U.S. inquiry-learning networks and programs. The authors review evidence on human cognitive architecture, working memory, expertise, and the comparative effectiveness of explicit instruction, worked examples, and guided discovery.

The main conclusion is that the broad reform agenda promoted by IBME is not justified by evidence. The paper argues that novice learners generally do not learn better when left to discover material without explicit teaching, that unassisted discovery is less effective than guided or explicit instruction, and that inquiry-based learning is not generally superior for fostering transfer or conceptual understanding. The authors also reject the claim that inquiry-based classrooms inherently solve equity problems, concluding that more direct, principled instruction is typically more effective for novice mathematics learners.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed critical commentary/scoping review synthesizing prior research rather than reporting a new empirical study. It uses cited meta-analyses and experiments, but the paper itself is not a primary causal evaluation and therefore only partially meets credibility criteria.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper argues for a substantial instructional implication—favor explicit instruction over inquiry for novice mathematics learning—but it does not report a new effect attributable to an intervention in K-12 contexts. Its practical impact is therefore indirect and unclear within the requested K-12 AI/tutoring framing.

finding.finding_summary: This is a critical review arguing that inquiry-based mathematics education (IBME) is not supported as a general reform for novice learners. It cites meta-analytic evidence that unassisted discovery underperforms explicit instruction (108 studies; mean d = -0.38, 95% CI [-0.50, -0.25]) and concludes that students learn mathematics better when they are explicitly taught rather than left to discover material on their own.
finding.measure: Learning gains, application/transfer test performance, and mastery of mathematical concepts in reviewed studies
finding.study_size: 108 studies (meta-analysis cited); additional single studies include n=80 and n=129

finding.finding_summary: The paper highlights an experimental study on the control-of-variables strategy (N=112) showing direct instruction substantially outperformed discovery learning for mastering scientific reasoning skills. In that study, 77% of students in the direct-instruction condition became masters versus 23% in discovery learning, and mastery transferred equally well to an authentic poster-evaluation task once mastery was achieved.
finding.measure: Mastery of control-of-variables strategy and transfer to science-fair poster evaluation

finding.finding_summary: Although the paper discusses transfer, problem solving, and conceptual understanding as important durable outcomes, its synthesis argues that inquiry/discovery is not superior for developing these skills in novices. Evidence reviewed suggests that explicit instruction and principle-oriented explanations better support transferable understanding than minimally guided inquiry, including a randomized study where lecture-first sequences outperformed problem-solving-first sequences by almost 50% on both application and transfer tests.
finding.measure: Transfer tests, application tests, and principle-oriented understanding
finding.study_size: 129 students in one cited RCT; additional studies summarized
